title: Anthropic gives outside AI watchdog “employee-like” access
content:
Anthropic has granted external evaluators “employee-like access” to assess the risks of its models, following through on a commitment to increase safeguards over concerns the technology could run catastrophically out of control.
METR, a nonprofit that has worked with leading labs including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in the Claude maker’s office with access to its hardware and internal systems.
A greater role for third-party evaluators is among the main concrete steps the labs have proposed in response to rising concern about the dangers more capable AI systems could pose to the economy, cyber security and humanity at large.
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei achieved a rare moment of unity with arch-rivals Sam Altman and Elon Musk in September when the OpenAI and SpaceX bosses rallied behind his proposal to embed external auditors in the leading labs.
Thursday’s announcement marks the first step to implementing these pledges. OpenAI has yet to lay out plans to bring in evaluators after Altman said Amodei’s proposals were a good idea.
“As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessment,” Anthropic said on Thursday. “We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work.”
Critics of Anthropic’s proposal to use evaluators have argued the arrangements could lead to conflicts of interest, pointing to issues in the accounting sector, and that greater government regulation is required.
Anthropic argued that sharing information publicly could benefit malicious actors or competitors and added that its evaluators will operate similarly to bank supervision, whereby regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks.

report.summary: Anthropic has embedded METR evaluators inside its offices with employee-like access to hardware and internal systems, marking a first step toward third-party AI safety audits.
report.background: Anthropic’s move comes as frontier models grow more capable and concerns rise about catastrophic risks, cyber misuse, economic disruption and loss of human control. Leading labs have floated third-party evaluators as a concrete safeguard beyond internal red-teaming and voluntary responsible-scaling policies. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed embedding external auditors in top labs, winning rare support from OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk. Anthropic’s announcement is the first implementation of that pledge; OpenAI has not yet detailed similar plans. The arrangement also reflects a broader debate over whether voluntary industry audits or government regulation should govern AI safety, and how much sensitive information labs can disclose without helping competitors or malicious actors.
key_points: METR, a nonprofit evaluator that has worked with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, now has a team embedded in Anthropic’s office. It can access the company’s hardware and internal systems, an arrangement Anthropic calls “employee-like access.” This is unusually deep third-party access for an AI lab and lets METR assess model risks from inside rather than through limited external testing.

The move follows a September proposal by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to embed external auditors in leading labs. OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceX’s Elon Musk backed the idea, a rare show of unity among rivals. Anthropic’s announcement is the first concrete step; OpenAI has not yet laid out its own evaluator plans.

Anthropic says stronger models require stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessment. It wants public accountability but cannot disclose all safety-relevant information, arguing that publication could aid malicious actors or competitors. It compares the evaluator model to bank supervision, where regulators place resident examiners inside large banks.

Critics argue embedded evaluators may face conflicts of interest, pointing to problems in the accounting industry, and say stronger government regulation is needed. The debate highlights tension between voluntary lab-led audits, which can move fast and access sensitive systems, and independent oversight that may be more adversarial but slower or less informed.
report.impact: Anthropic’s arrangement could set a precedent for how frontier labs prove safety claims. If METR’s embedded role produces credible reports, it may pressure OpenAI, Google and Meta to offer similar access and help shape emerging audit standards. For developers, it signals that model providers may face deeper external evaluation, documentation and safety gates before deployment, adding compliance work but potentially making risk claims more trustworthy. For regular users, the immediate benefit is stronger independent scrutiny of models they rely on, though one embedded team cannot guarantee safety or replace regulation. The main risk is that voluntary, lab-funded audits become a substitute for public oversight rather than a complement.
report.tools: Follow METR’s public evaluations and Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy. For hands-on safety testing, try Inspect, the UK AI Safety Institute’s open-source evaluation framework; EleutherAI’s lm-evaluation-harness for model benchmarks; Garak for LLM vulnerability scanning; and MLCommons’ AILuminate safety benchmarks. These tools let developers reproduce red-team tests and track how third-party audit practices evolve.
